Based on May/June 2025 · 9708/24 · Q2(a) 8 marks With the help of a formula, explain the meaning of price elasticity of demand and consider the significance to a firm of having price elastic or price inelastic demand for its product.
What the mark scheme wants
  • Knowledge (up to 3): it measures the responsiveness of changes in demand to changes in price (1); the correct formula (1); the meaning of price elastic and inelastic in terms of the percentage or proportionate response (1).
  • Analysis (up to 3): the impact of rising or falling prices on the demand for a firm's products when PED is inelastic (1) and when it is elastic (1), with both rising and falling prices considered.
  • Evaluation (up to 2): a valid judgement on the importance of the distinction between elastic and inelastic demand for the effect of price changes on sales, with a mark for assessing what a firm should do to influence demand or spending.
PlanFormula and meaning. Elastic: price cut raises revenue. Inelastic: price rise raises revenue. Judge: the firm should use elasticity, but other factors matter.
Knowledge (K)Application (A)Analysis (N)Evaluation (E)

Price elasticity of demand measures how responsive the quantity demanded is to a price change. It equals the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price. Demand is elastic if the quantity changes by a greater percentage than price, and inelastic if by a smaller percentage.

If demand is elastic, a fall in price may raise total revenue because the rise in quantity outweighs the lower price, while a rise in price may reduce revenue. If demand is inelastic, a rise in price may raise revenue because quantity falls by less than price rises, while a price cut would reduce revenue.

Knowing whether demand is elastic or inelastic is likely to be very useful in setting prices, as it suggests whether to raise or cut prices to increase revenue. But the estimate may be inaccurate and other factors, such as competitors' responses, could change the outcome.

Based on Feb/March 2024 · 9708/22 · Q3(a) 8 marks With the help of a formula, explain the meaning of income elasticity of demand and consider the extent to which a rise in income will increase the consumption of all goods and services.
What the mark scheme wants
  • Knowledge (up to 3): an accurate definition of YED (1), an accurate formula (1), and the difference between normal and inferior goods (1).
  • Analysis (up to 3): normal goods have a positive value (1); uses a diagram (an upward-sloping income demand curve) or the formula to show why a rise in income increases consumption of such goods (1), justified with an example (1).
  • Evaluation (up to 2): if the good is inferior, demand falls when income rises (1) as consumers switch to normal or luxury goods; the second mark is for a justified conclusion.
PlanDefine and formula. Normal: positive, demand rises. Inferior: negative, demand falls. Conclude: not all goods rise.
Knowledge (K)Application (A)Analysis (N)Evaluation (E)

Income elasticity of demand measures how responsive demand is to a change in income. It equals the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in income. Normal goods have a positive YED and inferior goods a negative one.

For a normal good such as foreign holidays, a rise in income raises demand, because consumers can afford more of them, so a positive YED shows that consumption increases as incomes rise.

Not all goods will rise. For an inferior good such as a basic own-brand product, a rise in income may lead consumers to switch to better goods, so consumption falls. Overall, a rise in income increases the consumption of normal goods but not of all goods and services.

Based on May/June 2023 · 9708/21 · Q3(a) 8 marks With the help of a formula, explain the meaning of cross elasticity of demand and consider which determinants are most important in establishing the size and sign of its coefficient.
What the mark scheme wants
  • Knowledge (up to 3): what cross elasticity of demand measures (1), the formula (1), and the distinction between positive and negative XED (1).
  • Analysis (up to 3): why XED can be positive, for substitutes (1); why it can be negative, for complements (1); and the determinants of its magnitude, where the closer the relationship between two products the greater the size of XED (1).
  • Evaluation (up to 2): a valid judgement on the relative importance of the determinants of the size and sign of XED (1) and a conclusion (1).
PlanFormula and meaning. Positive: substitutes. Negative: complements. Size: closeness of the relationship. Judge: closeness of relationship matters most for size; the nature of the link for sign.
Knowledge (K)Application (A)Analysis (N)Evaluation (E)

Cross elasticity of demand measures how responsive the demand for one good is to a change in the price of another. It equals the percentage change in quantity demanded of good X divided by the percentage change in the price of good Y. It is positive for substitutes and negative for complements.

XED is positive when goods are substitutes, because a higher price for Y makes consumers switch to X, and negative for complements, because a higher price for Y lowers demand for the good used with it. The closer the relationship, whether substitutes or complements, the larger the size of the coefficient.

The nature of the relationship, whether the goods are used together or in place of each other, is likely to determine the sign, while how close the substitutes are, and how the market is defined, may be most important for the size. A narrowly defined market is likely to give a larger coefficient.

Based on Oct/Nov 2023 · 9708/22 · Q2(a) 8 marks With the help of a formula, explain what is meant by the term price elasticity of demand for a product and consider the extent to which it allows an entrepreneur to determine the effect of price changes on the total expenditure on their product.
What the mark scheme wants
  • Knowledge (up to 3): a clear understanding of the meaning of PED (1), an accurate formula (1), and what price elastic and inelastic mean in terms of relative proportionate or percentage changes rather than large or small changes (1).
  • Analysis (up to 3): how total expenditure is affected by price changes if demand is elastic (up to 2) and if demand is inelastic (up to 2); both price increases and decreases should be considered, otherwise a maximum of 1 mark for that part.
  • Evaluation (up to 2): considering the extent to which the concept helps the entrepreneur to determine the effect.
PlanFormula and meaning. Elastic: price and expenditure move in opposite directions. Inelastic: same direction. Evaluate: estimates and other factors.
Knowledge (K)Application (A)Analysis (N)Evaluation (E)

Price elasticity of demand is the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price. Demand is elastic if the percentage change in quantity is greater than the percentage change in price, and inelastic if it is smaller.

If demand is elastic, a price rise leads to a larger percentage fall in quantity, so total expenditure falls, and a price cut raises total expenditure. If demand is inelastic, a price rise leads to a smaller percentage fall in quantity, so expenditure rises, and a price cut lowers it.

PED helps an entrepreneur predict the effect on expenditure, but only to the extent that the estimate is accurate. Elasticity can change along the demand curve and over time, and other factors such as rivals' prices may alter the outcome.

It will decrease by 12.5%.
It will increase by 2%.

mcq.why: 0.4 × (-5%) = -2%, so demand for Y falls by 2%.

Based on May/June 2020 · 9708/23 · Q2(a) 8 marks A new smartphone's price elasticity of supply is estimated at 0.8 in the short run and 1.5 in the long run. Explain price elasticity of supply and suggest why the two estimates differ.
What the mark scheme wantsUp to 2 marks for what price elasticity of supply measures and its formula. Up to 6 marks for applying the factors that explain the difference.

Price elasticity of supply measures the responsiveness of quantity supplied to a change in price. PES = percentage change in quantity supplied ÷ percentage change in price.

A value of 0.8 suggests that supply of the smartphone is price inelastic in the short run: quantity supplied is likely to change by a smaller percentage than price. In the short run at least one factor, such as factory capacity, is fixed. Firms may have little spare capacity and few stocks of the new model or its components.

A value of 1.5 suggests that supply is price elastic in the long run. With more time, firms could build capacity, train workers and secure more components, and new producers may enter. Resources are likely to be more mobile over a longer period, so output could respond proportionately more.

Common mistakeExplaining price elasticity of demand, or giving factors without linking them to the short run and the long run.

Based on May/June 2020 · 9708/22 · Q3(a) 8 marks Many countries faced a water shortage after a long spell of very dry weather. Explain whether you would expect the price elasticity of supply of water to be relatively elastic or relatively inelastic.
What the mark scheme wantsUp to 2 marks for the meaning and formula. Up to 3 marks for why supply might be elastic and up to 3 for why it might be inelastic.

Price elasticity of supply measures how responsive quantity supplied is to a change in price. It is the percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the percentage change in price.

Supply of water is likely to be price inelastic in a drought because rivers and reservoirs may be low, so a higher price cannot create much more water. New reservoirs, pipes or desalination plants may take years to build. Spare capacity is likely to be very limited.

Supply could be more elastic where water has been stored in reservoirs and can be released quickly. It could also be more elastic where pipelines allow water to be moved from wetter areas or desalination plants have spare capacity. Over a long period supply is likely to become more elastic as investment is made, although the weather may still limit it.

Common mistakeGiving only one side. The question word "whether" rewards both cases before a decision.

Based on May/June 2022 · 9708/21 · Q3(a) 8 marks Explain two factors that determine the price elasticity of supply of a manufactured product.
What the mark scheme wantsUp to 2 marks for the definition or formula. Up to 3 marks for each of two factors: 1 for naming it and 2 for explaining it.

Price elasticity of supply is the percentage change in quantity supplied of a product divided by the percentage change in its price. It shows how responsive producers are to a price change.

One factor is spare capacity. A manufacturer with idle machines and available workers could raise output quickly when price rises. Supply is therefore likely to be more price elastic than for a firm already at full capacity.

A second factor is the ability to hold stocks. Manufactured goods that are not perishable can often be stored and released when price rises. This is likely to make supply more elastic, although storage may be costly for large or fast-changing products.

Common mistakeNaming three or four factors briefly. Two developed factors earn the marks.

Based on May/June 2025 · 9708/22 · Q3(b) 12 marks Assess the extent to which knowledge of a product's price elasticity of supply is the most useful measure of elasticity to a firm needing to react quickly to changes in its market.
What the mark scheme wantsLevels marking: up to 8 marks for knowledge and analysis and up to 4 for evaluation. Compare price elasticity of supply with at least one other elasticity, in the context of reacting quickly, and reach a judgement.

Price elasticity of supply may be useful because it indicates how quickly and how far a firm can raise output when the market price changes. A firm that finds its supply is inelastic could hold more stock, keep spare capacity or use more flexible labour so that it can respond sooner. This may be of limited use where production takes a long time or the product is perishable.

Price elasticity of demand could be more useful where the firm must decide quickly how to change its price, because it indicates the likely effect on revenue. Estimates may be out of date if tastes or rival products have changed.

Income elasticity could matter more in a recession, and cross elasticity when a rival changes its price. Each could warn the firm of a shift in demand before output plans are changed.

Overall, price elasticity of supply is likely to be the most useful where the problem is how fast output can change. Another measure could be more useful where the main uncertainty is about demand, so the judgement depends on the source of the market change and the reliability of the data.

Common mistakeDescribing price elasticity of supply without comparing it, which leaves no basis for "most useful".

Based on Feb/March 2024 · 9708/22 · Q2(a) 8 marks With the help of a demand and supply diagram, explain how the introduction of an indirect tax affects equilibrium in a market and consider the extent to which the incidence of the tax will fall on the consumer.
What the mark scheme wants
  • Knowledge (up to 3): an accurate definition of an indirect tax (1); an accurate diagram with labelled axes and equilibrium price and quantity (1); understanding that indirect taxes are used to discourage consumption of demerit goods (1).
  • Analysis (up to 3): the diagram shows an indirect tax shifting the supply curve to the left (1), raising the price to the consumer (1) and reducing the quantity demanded (1).
  • Evaluation (up to 2): the incidence on the consumer depends on the price elasticity of demand: the more inelastic demand, the more of the tax is passed to the consumer (1), and a justified conclusion (1).
PlanDefine the tax. Diagram: supply left, price up, quantity down. Evaluate: incidence depends on PED.
Knowledge (K)Application (A)Analysis (N)Evaluation (E)

An indirect tax is a tax on spending, such as VAT or a duty on cigarettes, collected by the seller but ultimately paid by consumers or producers. On a diagram, the original equilibrium is where demand meets supply at P1 and Q1. Governments often use indirect taxes to discourage consumption of demerit goods.

The tax raises costs by a fixed amount for each unit, so the supply curve shifts to the left. The equilibrium price paid by consumers rises to P2 and the quantity falls to Q2.

How much of the tax falls on consumers depends on the price elasticity of demand. If demand is inelastic, consumers have few substitutes, so the price rises by nearly the whole tax and consumers bear most of it. If demand is elastic, producers absorb more of it. So the incidence is likely to fall mainly on consumers for goods such as cigarettes, but not for goods with close substitutes.

Based on May/June 2025 · 9708/21 · Q3(a) 8 marks With the help of a diagram, explain how changes in a subsidy can influence the price and quantity sold of a product in a market and consider how expenditure on a subsidy is affected by the price elasticity of demand for the product.
What the mark scheme wants
  • Knowledge (up to 3): a correct diagram with labelled axes, demand and supply (1); an increase in a subsidy shifting supply to the right, lowering price and raising quantity, with new equilibrium positions shown (1); a decrease in a subsidy shifting supply to the left, raising price and lowering quantity (1).
  • Analysis (up to 3): a subsidy is a sum of money paid by a government to a producer (1); an increase lowers the price charged to consumers and raises quantity (1) and the explanation of how that affects the cost to the government.
  • Evaluation (up to 2): the cost of a subsidy depends on price elasticity of demand: the more elastic, the more quantity rises and the greater the expenditure, with a justified conclusion.
PlanDiagram: subsidy shifts supply right, price down, quantity up. Cost = subsidy × quantity. Elastic demand: quantity rises more, so cost is higher.
Knowledge (K)Application (A)Analysis (N)Evaluation (E)

A subsidy is a payment by the government to producers per unit of output. On a diagram it shifts the supply curve to the right, by the amount of the subsidy, lowering the equilibrium price and increasing the quantity sold. A bigger subsidy shifts supply further, and removing it shifts supply back to the left, raising price and cutting quantity.

Because the subsidy lowers firms' costs, they supply more at each price, and the price consumers pay falls. The government pays the subsidy on every unit sold, so the cost is the subsidy per unit multiplied by the quantity sold after the subsidy.

The cost depends on the price elasticity of demand. If demand is elastic, the fall in price brings a large rise in quantity, so the total spent on the subsidy is larger. If demand is inelastic, quantity rises less, so the subsidy costs less but also does less to raise consumption.

Based on Oct/Nov 2021 · 9708/21 · Q3(a) 8 marks With the aid of a diagram, explain the consequences for consumers and producers of introducing a minimum price in the market for a product.
What the mark scheme wants
  • Knowledge (up to 2): a correct diagram with price and quantity axes labelled (1); a minimum price shown above the equilibrium, with demand and supply labelled (1).
  • Application (up to 3): consequences for consumers, who pay a higher price, which discourages consumption and is beneficial if the good is a demerit good.
  • Application (up to 3): consequences for producers, whose incomes may rise, but who face excess supply because consumers do not buy at the higher price, so government action may be needed to buy up or restrict the surplus.
PlanDiagram: minimum price above equilibrium. Consumers pay more, buy less. Producers: higher price but a surplus, government may buy it.
Knowledge (K)Application (A)Analysis (N)Evaluation (E)

A minimum price is a legal floor below which the price cannot fall. On a supply and demand diagram, with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis, it is shown as a horizontal line above the equilibrium price. At this price quantity supplied is greater than quantity demanded, so there is excess supply (a surplus).

Consumers face a higher price than in the free market, so the quantity demanded falls. This would be a benefit if the product were a demerit good, such as alcohol or tobacco, because consumption falls, but it is a cost to consumers who lose consumer surplus, and to poorer households if the good is a necessity, since they have less to spend on other goods. They also have less choice, because cheaper products disappear. Producers receive a higher price on each unit sold, so their revenue per unit may rise, and if demand is inelastic, their total revenue rises. Sellers also gain from stability of income, as in farming. But at the higher price there is excess supply: producers cannot sell all they would like to, so some may have to store the surplus or cut production, and there may be waste. Producers may also have less incentive to cut costs. If the government buys the surplus, taxpayers bear the cost.

Based on May/June 2023 · 9708/21 · Q3(b) 12 marks With the help of a diagram, assess whether the benefits of a buffer stock scheme for an agricultural product always outweigh its disadvantages.
What the mark scheme wants
  • Analysis (up to 8): a correctly labelled diagram showing a price band, with the agency buying in a good harvest and selling in a poor one; the benefits, such as stable prices and farm incomes, encouraging investment and long-term supply, and protecting consumers (up to 4); the disadvantages, such as the cost of buying and storing, spoilage, setting the band wrongly, running out of stock or money, and the opportunity cost (up to 4). Indicative content may include these points.
  • Evaluation (up to 4): a judgement on whether the benefits always outweigh the disadvantages, which may depend on the size of the stock, the length of the run of harvests and the price band, with a conclusion.
PlanDiagram with floor and ceiling. Benefits: stable prices, income, investment. Disadvantages: cost, run out, wrong band. Judge: not always.
Knowledge (K)Application (A)Analysis (N)Evaluation (E)

A buffer stock scheme is run by an agency that sets a minimum and a maximum price for an agricultural product. Agricultural prices fluctuate because supply depends on the weather and both supply and demand are price inelastic, so a small change in supply causes a large change in price.

On the diagram, with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis, there is a price band between the floor and the ceiling. In a good harvest, supply shifts right and the price would fall below the floor, so the agency buys the surplus to hold the price at the minimum, adding to its stock. In a poor harvest, supply shifts left and the price would rise above the ceiling, so the agency sells from its stock to hold the price at the maximum. The benefits are that prices and farm incomes are more stable, so farmers can plan and invest, which encourages long-term supply and may raise output. Consumers, particularly poor households, are protected from price spikes in essential foods, and the economy may benefit from more stable incomes.

The disadvantages are costly. The agency must pay to buy, store and handle the crop, and goods may perish, so there is waste. The band may be set wrongly: if the floor is too high, the agency accumulates huge stocks, and if the ceiling is too low, it runs out of stock. It may also run out of money. The funds have an opportunity cost, and farmers may produce too much of the supported crop. The scheme also needs good forecasts. The benefits do not always outweigh the disadvantages. They are more likely to outweigh them when the crop can be stored for a long time, the band is set close to the long-run equilibrium price and the agency has funds, as with grains. They are less likely to for perishable goods, or when the band is set badly. Overall, the benefits are greater for storable crops with well-managed schemes, but not always.

excess supply, no effect, no effect

mcq.why: A maximum above equilibrium has no effect, one below creates excess demand, and a minimum above equilibrium creates excess supply.

Based on May/June 2020 · 9708/23 · Q4(a) 8 marks Explain why the theory of comparative advantage may not give a true account of the benefits of free trade.
What the mark scheme wants
  • Knowledge (up to 2): a lower opportunity cost of producing a product because of differing resources (1), which leads to specialisation and trade (1).
  • Application (up to 6): consideration of reasons why the law of comparative advantage may not lead to benefits through trade, up to 2 marks for each reason explained, for example transport costs, trade barriers, immobility of factors, changing opportunity costs and over-specialisation.
PlanDefine comparative advantage (opportunity cost). Then three developed limits: transport costs, immobility, increasing opportunity costs or over-specialisation.
Knowledge (K)Application (A)Analysis (N)Evaluation (E)

A country has a comparative advantage in a good if it can produce it at a lower opportunity cost than another country because of its resources. It should specialise in that good and trade for others.

The benefits may be smaller than the theory suggests. Transport costs and tariffs raise the price of traded goods and can remove the gain. Factors are not perfectly mobile: workers who lose their jobs in one industry may not have the skills to move into another, so unemployment results. Opportunity costs may rise as a country specialises, because the best resources are used first, which weakens the advantage, and over-specialisation makes an economy vulnerable to a fall in the price of its main export.

Based on Feb/March 2025 · 9708/22 · Q4(a) 8 marks With the help of a formula, explain two reasons for an improvement in the terms of trade and consider the extent to which an improvement in the terms of trade will benefit an economy.
What the mark scheme wants
  • Knowledge (up to 3): an accurate definition of the terms of trade or an accurate formula (1); an improvement is likely if export prices rise (1) relative to import prices (1).
  • Analysis (up to 3): an improvement means a unit of exports buys relatively more imports (1), which may improve living standards (1) as imported goods appear cheaper (1), but it may lead to a current account deficit (1). Maximum 2 if only benefits are considered.
  • Evaluation (up to 2): an assessment of the advantages and disadvantages, for example in terms of unemployment and price elasticity values, with a valid conclusion.
PlanFormula: export price index ÷ import price index × 100. Two reasons: export prices rise, import prices fall. Benefit: more imports per export. Risk: less competitive, current account deficit. Judge using elasticity.
Knowledge (K)Application (A)Analysis (N)Evaluation (E)

The terms of trade are the ratio of an index of export prices to an index of import prices, multiplied by 100. An improvement occurs when export prices rise relative to import prices. This could be because world demand for the country's exports rises, pushing up their price, or because the price of imported raw materials falls.

An improvement means each unit of exports buys more imports, which may raise living standards because imported goods become relatively cheaper. But higher export prices can reduce export sales if foreign demand is price elastic, which could lead to a current account deficit.

Whether an improvement is beneficial depends on the price elasticity of demand for exports and on the effect on employment in export industries. If demand is inelastic, revenue from exports rises, so it is likely to be of overall benefit; if elastic, the loss of competitiveness may outweigh the gain.

Based on Oct/Nov 2024 · 9708/21 · Q5(a) 8 marks Explain the potential advantages of free trade and consider whether such advantages are always greater than the potential disadvantages of free trade.

  • Analysis (up to 3): at least two disadvantages and how they contrast with the advantages: specialisation could cause some sectors to run down, with higher unemployment; overreliance on some commodities is risky; there is a security risk if vital resources are imported.
  • Evaluation (up to 2): a valid judgement on whether the advantages are always greater than the disadvantages, with a conclusion.
PlanTwo advantages: world output, choice, living standards. Two disadvantages: unemployment in declining sectors, dependence. Judge: advantages usually bigger, but not always.
Knowledge (K)Application (A)Analysis (N)Evaluation (E)

Free trade allows countries to specialise in goods in which they have a comparative advantage, which raises world output. Consumers get a wider choice of goods at lower prices, and living standards can rise.

But free trade can cause some industries to decline when they cannot compete with cheaper imports, which raises unemployment in those sectors. Countries that specialise in a few commodities depend heavily on their prices, and relying on imports of vital resources may be a security risk.

The advantages are probably greater for most countries over time, because of higher output and lower prices, but they are not always greater: the costs fall on particular workers and regions and can be severe for developing countries that depend on one export.

Based on Oct/Nov 2022 · 9708/23 · Q4(a) 8 marks Explain how a higher rate of inflation in an economy compared to its trading partners and a decline in the exchange rate will each affect the terms of trade in an economy.
What the mark scheme wants
  • Knowledge (up to 2): the terms of trade measure the ratio of export to import prices (1) with an accurate formula, index of export prices ÷ index of import prices (1).
  • Application (up to 3): a higher rate of inflation than trading partners raises the relative price of exports (1) and reduces the relative price of imports (1), so the terms of trade improve (1).
  • Application (up to 3): a decline in the exchange rate reduces the relative price of exports (1) and raises the relative price of imports (1), so the terms of trade deteriorate (1).
PlanFormula. Higher relative inflation: export prices rise faster, ToT improve. Lower exchange rate: exports cheaper, imports dearer, ToT deteriorate.
Knowledge (K)Application (A)Analysis (N)Evaluation (E)

The terms of trade measure the ratio of export prices to import prices, calculated as the index of export prices divided by the index of import prices, multiplied by 100. A rise means that export prices have risen relative to import prices, so fewer exports are needed to buy a given quantity of imports.

If a country's rate of inflation is higher than that of its trading partners, its export prices rise faster than the prices of its imports, which are set partly abroad. The export price index rises relative to the import price index, so the terms of trade improve. A higher relative price of exports makes them less competitive, so the quantity sold may fall, which could worsen the trade balance, even though the terms of trade have improved. Domestic goods also become relatively dearer than imports. If the exchange rate declines, the effect is the opposite. Exports become cheaper in foreign currency, since each unit of foreign currency buys more of the domestic currency, so export prices in foreign currency fall. Imports become dearer in domestic currency, because more domestic currency is needed to buy the same foreign goods. The import price index rises relative to the export price index, so the terms of trade deteriorate. A deterioration is not necessarily bad if the lower export prices raise sales and improve the current account.

Based on May/June 2022 · 9708/23 · Q4(a) 8 marks Explain why some countries consistently have a deficit on the current account of the balance of payments.
What the mark scheme wants
  • Knowledge (up to 2): the current account is trade in goods, services plus other income (1); a deficit is where payments made by a country exceed payments received, or where income from exports is exceeded by expenditure on imports (1).
  • Application (up to 6): explanation of causes of a current account deficit (up to 3), such as an appreciation of the exchange rate, a reduced supply of primary goods for export, a deterioration in the terms of trade, reduced aid, reduced transfers from migrant workers and increased protection from trading partners; and why some countries may experience a persistent deficit (up to 3).
PlanDefine the current account and a deficit. Causes: high exchange rate, falling terms of trade, weak exports. Persistence: structural weaknesses such as low productivity.
Knowledge (K)Application (A)Analysis (N)Evaluation (E)

The current account of the balance of payments records trade in goods and services together with primary income (such as profits and interest) and secondary income (such as transfers and aid). A deficit means that payments made by the country exceed the payments it receives, so spending on imports and other outflows is greater than income from exports.

A country may have a persistent deficit for several reasons. If the exchange rate is too high, exports are dear for foreign buyers and imports are cheap, so the volume of exports falls and imports rise. If the terms of trade have deteriorated, because export prices fall relative to import prices, export earnings buy fewer imports. A country that depends on a few primary products, which earn little and whose prices fluctuate, may find that export revenue falls when prices drop. Weak competitiveness is another cause. If productivity is low or costs and inflation are higher than in competitor countries, domestic goods are less attractive and consumers buy imports instead. Strong consumer demand, for example when incomes are rising, may raise spending on imports faster than exports. Falls in aid, or in transfers sent home by migrant workers, or large payments of profits and interest on foreign debt, can also contribute, because they reduce income received or raise payments abroad.

Based on Oct/Nov 2023 · 9708/23 · Q5(b) 12 marks A country has a persistent deficit on the current account of its balance of payments. Assess the likely consequences for the domestic and external economy of this country.
What the mark scheme wants
  • Analysis (up to 8): what a persistent deficit means; the domestic consequences, such as employment, growth, inflation, living standards, the government budget, business confidence and a need to restructure the economy; and the external consequences, such as the exchange rate, ability to trade, need for imports and debt interest. Maximum Level 2 if only the domestic or only the external economy is considered.
  • Evaluation (up to 4): clearly considers the likely consequences for both parts of the economy and reaches a conclusion on the most likely consequences. A one-sided response cannot gain evaluation marks.
PlanDefine persistent deficit. Domestic: lower AD, output and jobs; contractionary policy. External: depreciation, debt, reserves. Judge by size and financing.
Knowledge (K)Application (A)Analysis (N)Evaluation (E)

A persistent deficit on the current account means that spending on imports, and payments of income and transfers abroad, exceed receipts year after year, so the country has to borrow, sell assets or run down reserves to pay for the gap.

The domestic consequences include lower net exports, which are a component of AD, so AD and output could be lower, with weaker growth and employment, particularly in exporting and import-competing industries. The government may feel pressure to adopt contractionary policies to reduce imports, which would cut growth and raise unemployment. Business confidence may fall and the economy may need to restructure towards industries that can compete. On the other hand, imports may raise living standards in the short run by providing cheaper goods and a wider choice, and the deficit may be financed by foreign investment that creates jobs.

The external consequences are on the exchange rate and finances. With a floating exchange rate, the currency is likely to depreciate as demand for it falls relative to supply, which raises the price of imports and may cause inflation, though it makes exports cheaper. With a fixed rate, the central bank must sell reserves, which could run out. The country may borrow from abroad, which increases external debt and the cost of interest payments, and its ability to buy needed imports may fall if lenders lose confidence. The seriousness depends on the size and the cause of the deficit. A deficit financed by investment from abroad in productive projects is less worrying than one that results from consumption of imports. How long it lasts and the strength of the economy matter too. Overall, a persistent deficit is likely to harm both the domestic and the external economy, but a small deficit financed by long-term investment can be sustained, whereas a large one that reflects weak competitiveness is likely to cause lasting problems.

Based on Oct/Nov 2024 · 9708/21 · Q5(b) 12 marks Assess whether an economy will always benefit from having a surplus on the current account of its balance of payments.
What the mark scheme wants
  • Analysis (up to 8): the potential benefits, such as surplus foreign exchange to invest abroad, more jobs in the export sector, more domestic purchasing and employment, and possible growth (up to 4); the potential disadvantages, such as weak domestic demand and lower employment, lower growth, a surplus caused by recession, and lower output and employment in deficit countries (up to 4).
  • Evaluation (up to 4): considers both the benefits and disadvantages, the size of the surplus and its possible causes, and concludes whether an economy will always benefit. A one-sided response cannot gain evaluation marks.
PlanBenefits: exchange earnings, export jobs, growth. Disadvantages: may reflect weak demand or recession; harm to partners. Judge by size and cause.
Knowledge (K)Application (A)Analysis (N)Evaluation (E)

A surplus means that a country earns more from exports and other income than it spends abroad. It could give the country foreign exchange to invest abroad or to build reserves, which provides a cushion in a crisis. High exports create jobs in the export sector and raise AD, since net exports are a component of AD, which could support growth. If imports are low because consumers buy domestic goods, domestic firms sell more and employment may rise. A surplus may also reflect strong competitiveness, which is attractive to investors.

However, a surplus does not always benefit the economy. It could be a sign of weak domestic demand: if consumers do not spend, imports are low, so the surplus arises together with low consumption, lower employment and slower growth. It might even be caused by a recession that cuts imports, in which case the surplus does not signal strength. A large surplus can mean that resources are devoted to exports rather than to raising living standards at home, and a high exchange rate caused by the surplus can reduce competitiveness. It also means deficits elsewhere, which could lead to lower output and employment in the deficit countries, and trade tensions.

An economy will not always benefit. A surplus caused by strong competitiveness and growing exports is likely to be beneficial, particularly if it raises output and employment. A surplus caused by weak domestic demand or recession is much less beneficial. The size of the surplus and how long it lasts matter too: a modest surplus is likely to be helpful, but a very large and persistent one could create problems. Overall, a current account surplus is likely to benefit an economy when it reflects growing exports and competitiveness, but it is not always beneficial, since the cause of the surplus and its effect on domestic demand determine the outcome.

May/June 2024 · 9708/41 and 43 · Q3 20 marks With the help of an indifference curve diagram, assess the extent to which a rise in price would affect the demand for a normal good differently from the demand for a Giffen good.
What the mark scheme wants
  • Analysis (14): a diagram with indifference curves, budget lines and price lines; the budget line moves because of the price rise; the path of consumption shows the substitution and income effects for a normal good and a Giffen good; comment on overall demand from the two effects. No diagram: Level 2 at most.
  • Evaluation (6): the extent of the change depends on the price elasticity of demand, and on the slope of the indifference curve (the marginal rate of substitution).
Diagram to drawTwo diagrams side by side with the same layout. In each: original budget line and equilibrium A; new, steeper budget line (price rise) and equilibrium B; dashed compensating line and point C. For the normal good, B is left of A. For the Giffen good, the large negative income effect puts B to the right of A.
KANE

An indifference curve shows all the combinations of two goods that give a consumer the same satisfaction, and a budget line shows the combinations the consumer can afford with a given income and given prices. The consumer is in equilibrium where the budget line is a tangent to the highest indifference curve the consumer can reach. A rise in the price of a good pivots the budget line inwards, and the change in quantity demanded can be split into a substitution effect and an income effect.

A rise in price is likely to reduce the demand for a normal good because both effects work in the same direction. The substitution effect moves the consumer along the original indifference curve towards the relatively cheaper good, so less of the dearer good is bought. The fall in real income then lowers consumption of a normal good further, so the income effect also reduces quantity demanded. The demand curve slopes downward.

For a Giffen good the effects are likely to work in opposite directions. The substitution effect still reduces consumption, but the fall in real income causes the consumer to buy more of the good because it is inferior, as the consumer can no longer afford better alternatives. If this negative income effect is larger than the substitution effect, quantity demanded rises when the price rises, and the demand curve slopes upward. This is a possible outcome for a very poor household that spends much of its income on a staple food. Giffen goods appear to be very rare, so for most goods the effect of a price rise is likely to be the same as for a normal good.

The extent of the difference depends on the price elasticity of demand. For a normal good a price rise could cause a large or small fall in demand depending on how many substitutes exist. It also depends on the slope of the indifference curves, which show the marginal rate of substitution: the more easily the consumer can swap one good for another, the larger the substitution effect and the more likely it is to outweigh the income effect. Overall, a rise in price is likely to affect the demand for a normal good very differently from a Giffen good only where the income effect is large and negative. In most markets the difference is small, but it is real in theory and helps to explain why a demand curve may not always slope downward.

May/June 2024 · 9708/41 and 43 · Q2 20 marks The long-term equilibrium position in perfect competition is frequently used to illustrate efficient resource allocation in a free market economy. Explain why this is so and consider what prevents efficiency from being achieved.
What the mark scheme wants
  • Analysis (14): allocative and productive efficiency; a diagram or explanation of long-run equilibrium in perfect competition; the barriers to efficiency: market failure (excessive profits, very large investments needed, externalities, merit goods, need for public goods) and how government intervention (regulation, taxation, subsidies, ownership) might help.
  • Evaluation (6): allocative and productive efficiency are mainly theoretical and depend on precise marginal calculations; intervention does not always work (government failure).
Diagram to drawA perfectly competitive firm in the long run: horizontal AR = MR at the price, MC cutting through the minimum of AC at the same point. Label P = MC (allocative) and AC at its minimum (productive).
KANE

Allocative efficiency occurs when resources are allocated to the goods consumers value most, which happens where price equals marginal cost, so that total satisfaction is maximised. Productive efficiency occurs when output is produced at the lowest possible average cost, at the minimum point of the average cost curve.

The long-term equilibrium in perfect competition illustrates efficient resource allocation because the firm achieves both types of efficiency. Firms are price takers, so the firm's average revenue equals its marginal revenue. Profit is maximised where MR equals MC, so price equals marginal cost, which gives allocative efficiency. Supernormal profits attract new firms, which shifts supply right and lowers the price until only normal profit is made, so price equals average cost. With free entry and exit this is likely to happen at the minimum of the average cost curve, where MC cuts AC, so the firm also achieves productive efficiency. This may only hold in the long run and under the strict assumptions of perfect competition, such as homogeneous products and perfect information.

Several features of real markets could prevent efficiency from being achieved. Where there are external costs, such as pollution, the firm ignores the cost to third parties, so the market output is higher than the socially efficient output and allocative efficiency is not achieved at the social level. Public goods such as street lighting would not be provided by the market because of the free rider problem, and merit goods such as education could be under-consumed. Where a very large investment is needed, one firm may dominate the market and earn excessive profit with a price above marginal cost. A government could respond with a tax on the polluter, a subsidy for education, direct provision of street lighting or regulation of a dominant firm.

However, the concepts of allocative and productive efficiency are mainly theoretical because they depend on precise calculations of marginal changes and costs. Government intervention may also fail if the government has poor information or sets the tax at the wrong level, so it does not necessarily achieve efficiency. Overall, perfect competition is a useful benchmark that illustrates why price equal to marginal cost is efficient, but real markets are unlikely to meet its conditions, and the cures for market failure may themselves be imperfect.

Feb/March 2023 · 9708/42 · Q2 20 marks The use of air travel leads to market failure caused by negative externalities. With the help of a diagram, assess the extent to which a government can intervene to correct this market failure.
What the mark scheme wants
  • Analysis (14): market failure as allocative inefficiency: define allocative efficiency and link to maximising consumer satisfaction; a diagram of output where AR = MC consistent with efficiency. Define a negative externality (cost to society greater than that borne by the individual: a "spill-over"). A labelled diagram showing the market equilibrium, the allocatively efficient output and the welfare loss. Forms of intervention: taxation (raises the cost of flying, lowers demand and the number of flights), negative advertising, direct regulation.
  • Evaluation (6): how well each form of intervention works and what limits it (information about the size of the externality, effects on employment and tourism, whether the tax is set at the right level).
Diagram to drawDemand (MPB = MSB), MPC and MSC above it. Mark Qm and Qs, the prices, and the welfare loss triangle. Show the tax shifting MPC up to MSC.
KANE

A negative externality occurs when the production or consumption of a good imposes a cost on a third party that is not paid by the producer or consumer, so the marginal social cost is greater than the marginal private cost. Allocative efficiency occurs where marginal social benefit equals marginal social cost, so that resources are allocated to maximise society's satisfaction.

Air travel is likely to lead to market failure because airlines and passengers ignore the cost of emissions and noise. On a diagram the market equilibrium is where demand (MPB) meets the airlines' marginal private cost (MPC), at output Qm. The marginal social cost curve lies above MPC by the external cost per flight, and the socially efficient output Qs is where MSB equals MSC. Because Qm is greater than Qs, the market over-produces and there is a welfare loss, shown by the triangle between MSC and MSB. The size of the welfare loss depends on how large the external cost is, which is difficult to measure.

A government could use a tax to correct the failure. A tax per flight equal to the external cost shifts the supply curve up to MSC, raises the price paid by passengers and reduces the number of flights to Qs, so allocative efficiency is achieved and the externality is internalised. A government could also use negative advertising to reduce demand, or regulation such as limits on night flights or emissions standards. A tax may not be fully effective if it is set at the wrong level because the external cost is hard to estimate, or if demand for flights is inelastic so that the number of flights falls little. It could also reduce employment and tourism income.

Regulation may give more precise control over noise or emissions but could be costly to monitor, and negative advertising may have a small effect on behaviour. Intervention may also suffer from government failure, such as time lags and lobbying by the industry. Overall, a government is likely to be able to reduce the market failure substantially through a combination of a tax and regulation, but it is unlikely to eliminate it because the external cost is difficult to measure and each policy has its own costs.

Oct/Nov 2021 · 9708/43 · Q4(b) 13 marks 'In large firms the long-run average cost falls as output increases and consumers benefit from lower prices. In small firms it does not. There is, therefore, no place in a modern economy for small firms.' Do you agree with these statements?
What the mark scheme wants
  • Whether costs necessarily fall as output rises (economies then diseconomies).
  • Whether consumers necessarily benefit if costs fall.
  • Whether there is no place for small firms: the purpose and reasons for small firms.
  • A conclusion about the statement as a whole.
LevelWhat earns it
L4 (9–13)Clear analysis and discussion of all parts, including the purpose and reasons for small firms, and a conclusion.
L3 (7–8)Two of the three parts developed, or all three with little analysis.
L2 (5–6)Mostly economies of scale and falling costs, the rest not considered in detail.
L1 (1–4)Some basic correct facts, with irrelevance and errors.
KANE

In large firms the long-run average cost may fall as output increases because of economies of scale. Economies of scale are the fall in LRAC as a firm grows, for example through bulk buying, specialist machinery and cheaper finance. However, LRAC does not fall for ever. Beyond the minimum efficient scale, communication and coordination problems could create diseconomies of scale and push LRAC up, so large firms do not always have lower costs.

Consumers may benefit from lower prices if large firms pass on their lower costs. A supermarket chain facing strong competition could cut prices to keep its customers. But if a large firm has market power it could keep the savings as profit, or raise prices, so the benefit to consumers is not certain.

There is likely to be a place for small firms in a modern economy because many of them do not compete on cost alone. A local café or a craft brewery may offer personal service, a distinctive product or local knowledge that customers value, so they may accept a higher price. Where the minimum efficient scale is small compared with the market, small firms can reach the lowest cost, and many can exist side by side. Small firms may also be flexible and innovative, and supply parts to large firms. This may not be enough where a small firm sells a standard product and a large rival can undercut it.

In conclusion, the statements are only partly correct. Costs may fall for large firms up to a point, consumers may benefit if savings are passed on, but the claim that there is no place for small firms is unlikely to hold in markets with niche demand or a small minimum efficient scale.

Based on Feb/March 2021 · 9708/42 · Q3(b) 13 marks A student claims that perfect competition delivers economic efficiency and monopoly does not. How far do you agree?
What the mark scheme wants
  • Explain allocative, productive and dynamic efficiency. Compare the perfectly competitive firm in the long run (allocative and productive efficiency) with a monopoly (potentially less efficient outcomes).
  • Dynamic efficiency may be possible for monopoly (supernormal profit to invest), but not for the competitive firm; and a monopoly might suffer from X-inefficiency. Assess the view.
KANE

Economic efficiency includes allocative efficiency, where price equals marginal cost, productive efficiency, where output is produced at the lowest average cost, and dynamic efficiency, where costs fall over time because of investment and innovation.

A firm in perfect competition is likely to achieve allocative and productive efficiency in the long run. As a price taker it maximises profit where MC equals the market price, so price equals marginal cost. Free entry and exit remove supernormal profit, so the firm ends at the minimum of its average cost curve. A monopoly sets MR equal to MC and charges a price above marginal cost, producing less than the allocatively efficient output, and its average cost could be above the minimum. This leads to a deadweight welfare loss.

The view may be too simple. A perfectly competitive firm earns only normal profit in the long run, so it is unlikely to have the funds for research and development, which makes dynamic efficiency less likely. A monopoly earns supernormal profit that could be reinvested, and it may enjoy economies of scale that lower its costs. A monopoly may also be X-inefficient because it faces no competitive pressure, so its costs could be higher than necessary. Overall, the view is partly correct on static efficiency, but a monopoly could be efficient in other ways, and perfect competition is rare, so the claim that a monopoly will not achieve economic efficiency is too strong.

May/June 2025 · 9708/42 · Q3 20 marks With the help of a diagram, assess whether the impact of an increase in labour productivity on the wages and employment of a firm is likely to be greater in a perfectly competitive labour market than in an imperfectly competitive labour market.
What the mark scheme wants
  • Analysis (14): a diagram; the impact of higher productivity (MPP, so MRP) on wages and employment in both types of market; and a judgement of which is greater, with reference to both wages and employment.
  • Evaluation (6): perfect competition rests on unrealistic assumptions (perfect mobility, identical labour, perfect knowledge); productivity is hard to measure, especially in services; training costs and skill differences challenge the model; productivity could come from replacing labour with capital, causing unemployment; the effect on jobs depends on how easily capital can substitute for labour; in an imperfect market some gains may pass to wages but the costs of raising productivity may cancel them.
Diagram to drawTwo diagrams side by side. Left: a perfectly competitive firm with a horizontal wage line and the MRP curve shifting right. Right: a monopsony with ACL, MCL and the MRP shift. Mark the old and new employment and wage in each.
KANE

Marginal revenue product (MRP) is the extra revenue from employing one more worker, equal to marginal physical product multiplied by marginal revenue. A profit-maximising firm in a perfectly competitive labour market is a wage taker and hires where MRP equals the wage, while a firm in an imperfectly competitive labour market, such as a monopsony, faces an upward sloping supply curve and hires where MRP equals the marginal cost of labour. An increase in labour productivity raises MPP and so shifts the MRP curve to the right in both cases.

In a perfectly competitive labour market the firm can hire as many workers as it wants at the market wage, so the supply of labour to the firm is horizontal. The rightward shift of MRP raises employment, with the wage unchanged for the individual firm, because the firm cannot influence the market wage. If the productivity rise happens across the whole industry, demand for labour in the market rises and the market wage could also rise, so wages in a perfectly competitive industry might increase in the long run.

In a monopsony the supply curve slopes upwards, so more workers can only be hired by paying a higher wage to all of them. The shift in MRP raises employment where the new MRP meets MCL, and the wage, read from the supply curve at the higher employment, also rises. However, the wage is still below the worker's MRP, and the rise in employment is smaller than in the competitive case because the firm must pay more to attract each extra worker.

The assumptions behind the competitive model, such as perfect mobility and identical workers, are unlikely to hold, and productivity is hard to measure in services such as health and education. Training to raise productivity costs money and could increase skill differences between workers. If productivity rises because firms use more machines in place of labour, employment could fall rather than rise. Overall, the effect on employment is likely to be greater in a perfectly competitive market, where the supply of labour to the firm is horizontal, while the effect on the firm's wage is likely to be greater in an imperfect market, where some of the gain may pass to workers. The extent depends on how easily capital can substitute for labour and on how the costs of raising productivity are shared.

May/June 2021 · 9708/42 · Q4 25 marks Evaluate whether the theory of wage determination can account for wage differentials (i) between a director and a general worker in the same company and (ii) between two workers doing the same job in different companies.
What the mark scheme wants
  • The theory of wages from demand and supply: demand from marginal productivity (MRP) and the price or marginal revenue of the product; supply from income and substitution effects leading to market supply. The theory assumes perfect markets.
  • Comment on the elasticities of demand and supply.
  • Real-world limits: imperfect competition, imperfect information, lack of labour mobility, discrimination, monopsony, trade union intervention, minimum wage boards.
  • Level 4 (18 to 25): MRP theory and labour supply, some elasticities, both (i) and (ii) addressed, imperfections used to account for differences. Conclusion for 22 to 25.
PlanTheory first (diagram: demand and supply). (i) Director: high MRP and scarce skills, inelastic supply; may also be set by a board. (ii) Same job, different firms: different MRP (firm productivity, product price), local supply, mobility and information. Then imperfections. Conclude: the theory explains much but not all.
KANE

The theory of wage determination says that the wage in a competitive labour market is set where the demand for labour meets the supply of labour. Demand comes from the marginal revenue product (MRP) of workers, which depends on their marginal physical product and the price the firm receives. Supply comes from workers' choices between work and leisure and the number of workers who choose each occupation.

The theory could account for the difference between a director and a general worker. A director's decisions can affect the revenue of the whole company, so the MRP is likely to be much higher. There are also few people with the skills, experience and training to be a director, so the supply of labour is small and inelastic. A high demand meeting an inelastic supply gives a high wage, and much of it may be economic rent. However, a director's MRP is very hard to measure because success depends on a team, and a director's pay is often set by a board that the director may influence, so it may not follow the competitive model closely.

The theory could also account for differences between two workers doing the same job in different companies. A programmer at a very productive firm that sells high-priced software has a higher MRP than a programmer at a firm with lower prices or lower productivity, so the first firm is likely to pay more. Local labour supply also matters: a firm in a city with few suitable workers may need to offer more. But in a perfectly competitive market workers could move to the higher-paying firm until wages equalised. Persistent differences suggest imperfections such as poor information, geographical immobility, discrimination, or a monopsony employer in one area.

Trade unions and minimum wage laws can also keep pay different from the market level, and workers may value non-wage benefits differently, so the same wage may not mean the same net advantage. Overall, the theory is likely to explain much of the difference between a director and a general worker through MRP and scarcity, and part of the difference between similar workers in different firms. The remaining differences are likely to come from market imperfections, so the theory is a useful but incomplete account.

Feb/March 2024 · 9708/42 · Q3 20 marks The introduction of a trade union into a perfectly competitive labour market will always lead to higher wage levels and a higher level of unemployment. With the help of a diagram, evaluate this statement.
What the mark scheme wants
  • Analysis (14): the characteristics of a perfectly competitive labour market; the role and main aims of a union, with the importance of wage bargaining; a diagram showing how the wage and employment are set in a perfectly competitive labour market and what happens in the firm; alternative ways a union might affect wages and employment, with reference to factors affecting demand and supply; the extent to which a union can influence wage and employment levels. Level 2 maximum without an accurate diagram.
  • Evaluation (6): "always" is the word to challenge: a union can raise wages without job losses if it raises productivity, or if demand is inelastic, or if the union wage is not above equilibrium.
KANE

In a perfectly competitive labour market there are many employers and many identical workers, labour is mobile, information is perfect and firms are wage takers, so the wage is set where the demand for labour (MRP) meets the supply of labour. A trade union is an organisation of workers that bargains collectively over pay and conditions, and it aims to raise wages, protect jobs and improve conditions.

A union may raise wages above the equilibrium wage, and if it does, unemployment is likely to follow. On a diagram with equilibrium wage W1 and employment Q1, a union wage W2 above W1 reduces the quantity of labour demanded to Q2, because each worker now costs more than they add to revenue at the old level of employment. The higher wage also attracts more people to offer their labour, so the quantity supplied rises to Q3. The gap Q2 to Q3 is unemployment. Union members who keep their jobs gain, while those who lose them, and those who cannot get a job, lose. How many jobs are lost depends on how elastic the demand for labour is: if firms can easily replace labour with machines, the loss will be larger, while if the demand is inelastic the loss could be small.

But a union will not always lead to both higher wages and higher unemployment. If the union negotiates better training, motivation and conditions, productivity could rise, which increases MPP and so MRP and shifts the demand for labour to the right. At the higher wage the firm may then employ as many workers as before, or more. Higher demand for the product would have the same effect. A union may also fail to raise wages if it is weak or if there are many non-union workers, so the wage stays at equilibrium.

In practice few labour markets are perfectly competitive, and in a monopsony a union could raise both wages and employment. Higher wages could also lead firms to raise prices or move production, which could reduce employment further in the long run. Overall, a union in a perfectly competitive market is likely to raise wages for those who keep their jobs and is likely to cause some unemployment unless it also raises productivity, so the claim that it will always lead to both is too strong.

Feb/March 2025 · 9708/42 · Q3 20 marks With the help of a diagram, evaluate the consequences of imposing an effective minimum wage on the employment level and the wage level in a monopsony labour market.
What the mark scheme wants
  • Analysis (14): a monopsony diagram with MRP, ACL (supply) and MCL; the wage and employment before the minimum wage; the effect of an effective minimum wage on both.
  • Evaluation (6): the effect depends on the relative elasticities of demand and supply in a monopsony; the size of the rise decides the impact; a higher wage might raise productivity (MRP shifts right) and so raise wages further; a minimum wage may close small, struggling firms and cut employment; higher costs may make firms less competitive globally; the effect on employment depends on how easily capital can substitute for labour; a conclusion on the likely net effect.
Diagram to drawMRP, ACL and MCL. Mark the monopsony employment where MCL = MRP and the wage on ACL. Draw the minimum wage line between the monopsony wage and the competitive wage: employment rises to where MRP (or supply) meets it. Add a second line above the competitive wage to show the fall.
KANE

A monopsony is a market with a single buyer of labour, so the employer faces the whole upward sloping supply curve of labour (the average cost of labour) and must raise the wage to all workers to hire one more. A minimum wage is a legal floor on pay, and it is effective if it is set above the wage the market would otherwise pay.

Without a minimum wage the monopsonist hires where marginal cost of labour equals marginal revenue product, at employment Q1, and pays the wage W1 read from the supply curve, which is below MRP. An effective minimum wage W2 above W1 means the firm cannot pay less than W2 to any worker, so the marginal cost of an extra worker is the minimum wage until supply runs out. The firm now hires up to the point where MRP equals W2, so employment rises to Q2 and the wage rises from W1 to W2, provided W2 is below the competitive wage.

If the minimum wage is set above the competitive wage, the result changes. MRP is below the minimum wage for the marginal workers, so employment falls below the competitive level and, if it is also below Q1, below the monopsony level. The quantity supplied is greater than the quantity demanded, so there is unemployment. The impact therefore depends on the size of the rise and on the elasticities of demand for and supply of labour in the market.

Other effects may change the outcome. A higher wage might increase productivity through better motivation and lower turnover, shifting MRP to the right and supporting even higher wages. However, higher costs could force small firms with low profit to close, or make firms less competitive against foreign producers, and employment may fall if firms can easily replace workers with machines. Overall, an effective minimum wage in a monopsony is likely to raise both the wage and employment if it is set between the monopsony and competitive wages, but the benefit is less certain if it is set too high or if firms can substitute capital for labour. The government needs good information on the monopsony wage, which is hard to estimate.
